book_title: The Salt Stones: Seasons of a Shepherd's Life
subject_line: Giono's stars and the flock at Knoll Farm
email_body:
Dear Helen,

I read about The Salt Stones and was struck that its title and epigraphs come from Jean Giono's The Serpent of Stars, while the book itself grounds that lyricism in more than two decades of lambing, shearing and coyote watches with your Icelandic sheep at Knoll Farm.

I'd love to ask what Giono gave you that a purely practical account of shepherding could not.

subject_line: Music and the spiritual in Strange Hymn
email_body:
Dear Carlene,

Congratulations on the Vermont Book Award for Strange Hymn. I read that the title grew out of your curiosity about how music and language connect the physical and the spiritual, and reviewers note how the poems blur history and myth, love and grief, song and silence.

I'd be glad to ask how sound and song shape your revisions, and whether any poem in the book began as something closer to music than to language.

subject_line: Bernie O'Dea's fourth case in Dying for News

book_title: Most Honorable Son: A Forgotten Hero's Fight Against Fascism and Hate During World War II
subject_line: Ben Kuroki, from a Hershey farm to the skies over Japan
email_body:
Dear Gregg,

Congratulations on Most Honorable Son winning the 2025 Nebraska Book Award for biography. Ben Kuroki's path, from a farm near Hershey, Nebraska, to becoming the only Japanese American to fly combat missions over Japan, is remarkable, and so is the fact that his story had slipped so far from public memory.

I'd like to ask how you first came across Kuroki, and what it took to rebuild a life that so few records had kept in view.

book_title: Into Whooperland: A Photographer's Journey with Whooping Cranes
subject_line: Following the cranes up the middle in Into Whooperland
email_body:
Dear Michael,

Into Whooperland follows the western whooping crane flock between Aransas on the Texas coast and Wood Buffalo in Canada by small plane rather than staying at either end. I read that you wanted to connect the dots up the middle.

I'd love to ask what those flights showed you about the Plains stretch of the route that you couldn't see from the ground.

book_title: White Flights: Race, Fiction, and the American Imagination
subject_line: The idea of white flight in White Flights
email_body:
Dear Jess,

I've been thinking about White Flights, your Graywolf collection that reads American fiction through the lens of race, and how the title turns a phrase about suburbs into a question about where the literary imagination chooses to go. It sits interestingly beside your novels, Your Face in Mine and The New Earth.

I'd like to ask how writing those essays changed the way you approach your own fiction.

subject_line: A tenth collection: The End of the Clockwork Universe
email_body:
Dear Fleda,

I noticed that The End of the Clockwork Universe, out from Carnegie Mellon University Press in 2025, is your tenth collection of poems. The title announces the end of the old wound-up, ticking universe, a striking frame for a book this far into a long body of work.

I'd like to ask what the title means to you, and how your sense of a collection has changed since your years as Delaware's poet laureate.

subject_line: The two languages of ʻĀina Hānau / Birth Land
email_body:

subject_line: Writing For Want of Water from El Paso
email_body:
Dear Sasha,

I came to For Want of Water through its National Poetry Series selection by Gregory Pardlo, and the title stayed with me, since it names a lack that feels especially sharp in a desert city like El Paso, where you teach in UTEP's bilingual MFA program.

I'd like to ask how place, and the experience of teaching writers who move between two languages, shaped the poems in the book and what you are writing now.

subject_line: The motion inside the title Still Falling
email_body:
Dear Jennifer,

The title of Still Falling, your 2023 Graywolf collection, holds a quiet paradox, the word still meaning both motionless and continuing. I was also interested to learn that you teach both poetry and translation at the University of Rochester while directing the Bread Loaf Writers' Conferences.

I'd like to ask how translating other poets has changed your ear for your own lines, and whether that shows up in this book.
